name: Marama
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Kanyoro, Rachel M.A. 1983. Unity in Diversity: A Linguistic Survey of the Abaluyia of Western Kenya — covers Marama among Luhya varieties, plausibly incl. phonology; not reached online

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. personal site (sites.google.com/site/michaelrmarlo), Luyia Dictionary Project site, and Diercks' papers page (mjkd.sites.pomona.edu/papers) — checked for Marama materials.
sources.note: No Marama paper, handout, wordlist or sketch is listed on any of the three sites (Marlo's papers folder itself is a sign-in Google Drive).

sources.citation: Osotsi, Eric M. 2020. A systematic reconstruction of the phonology of Proto-Luyia: a comparative analysis. MA thesis, University of Nairobi. hdl 11295/154048.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Marama [JE32C] only listed among northern Luyia dialects; not one of the seven sampled dialects; segmental reconstruction only; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Mulama, George Nanjira. 2019. The phonological processes in Olumarama: NC effects and vowel hiatus. MA thesis, Kenyatta University.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The only dedicated phonological description of Marama located; its language-background/phoneme-inventory chapter is the likeliest place for a tone/stress statement (even if the body is segmental).

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143. doi:10.3406/aflin.2014.1027 (per-page Persée text held by sibling check).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Marama does not occur in the article; verb tone melodies of other Luyia varieties; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Khachula, Annet A. 2013. Semantic shift in Lumarama: a lexical pragmatics approach. MA project, Dept. of Linguistics and Languages, University of Nairobi. 90 pp. hdl 11295/60019.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 1.1 'Background to the language' (pp. 2-3) is ethnographic/geographic only; the words tone/stress/accent never occur in a linguistic sense.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2009. Luyia tonal dialectology. Talk handout, Dept. of Linguistics and Languages, University of Nairobi, 16 Dec 2009. 15 pp. (Internet Archive copy of sites.google.com/site/michaelrmarlo/papers-1/)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No Marama data. p.12 lists Marama among Luyia dialects 'which have no documentation of their tonal systems (e.g., Kabarasi, Kisa, Marama, Nyala-East, and Tsotso)'. Nothing on stress anywhere in the handout.

sources.citation: Kanyoro, Rachel Msimbi Angogo. 1983. Unity in diversity: a linguistic survey of the Abaluyia of western Kenya (Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 20). Wien: Afro-Pub. 322 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Dialect survey covering Marama with phonological comparison of all Luyia varieties; the source the earlier scan named; may contain a general prosody (tone/stress) statement applying to Marama.

sources.citation: Heine, Bernd & Wilhelm J. G. Möhlig. 1980. Language and dialect atlas of Kenya, vol. 1: Geographical and historical introduction. Berlin: Reimer.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Kenyan dialect atlas with short structural notes on Luyia dialects including Marama; low chance of a prosody remark.

sources.citation: Sample, Ward Arthur. 1976. The application of rules in the phonology of Olukisa. PhD dissertation, Indiana University.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: online with a university library login
sources.note: Full phonology of Kisa, Marama's closest sister in the Kisa-Marama-Tsotso node; would give the nearest first-hand prosodic statement if nothing Marama-specific exists (different glottocode: Kisa).
